title: Senses of 'being able' (3): through justifying love
source_text: XIII. Tertio, ex ejusdem Doctoris sententia, dicimur multo plenius propinquiusque per charitatem, per quam homo justificatur, posse quae pertinent ad veram pietatem. Idque quia charitas seu dilectio ista, non est aliud quam voluntas seu volitio bona; quae quamdiu deest nobis, impossibile est bene vivere, quum autem adest, posse dicimur. Charitas autem per quam datur bene operandi potestas, varios gradus & incrementa habet, secundum quae potestas illa vel major, vel minor est: & initio infirma existens, nec ad omnia bona opera sufficiens, paulatim crescit, donec eo usque virium adolescat, ut cuncta invitantia, cuncta minantia, cuncta cruciantia superentur.
pass_a_gloss: XIII. Thirdly, from the opinion of the same Doctor, we are said much more fully and nearer through charity, through which man is justified, to be able to do the things which pertain to true piety. And that because that charity or love, is nothing other than a good will or volition; which as long as it is lacking to us, it is impossible to live well, but when it is present, we are said to be able. But charity through which the power of working well is given, has various degrees and increments, according to which that power is either greater, or less: and existing weak at the beginning, nor sufficient for all good works, little by little grows, until it grows up to such a point of strength, that all inviting things, all threatening things, all tormenting things are overcome.
pass_b_english: Thesis XIII. Third, in the same doctor's view, we are said in a much fuller and closer sense to be able to do what belongs to true devotion through the love by which a person is justified. That love is simply a good will, a good act of willing; while we lack it we cannot live rightly, and when we have it we are said to be able to.

The love that confers the power of doing good has various degrees and stages of growth, and the power is greater or lesser accordingly. Weak at first and not equal to every good work, it grows gradually until it gains enough strength to overcome every allurement, every threat and every torment.

lemmas.latin: cuncta invitantia, cuncta minantia, cuncta cruciantia superentur
lemmas.gloss: all inviting things, all threatening things, all tormenting things are overcome

choices.why: Caritas, the habitual theological virtue: 'love' in the reading, 'charity' in the literal pass.

bible_refs: Cornelius Jansenius, Augustinus (Louvain, 1640), tome 3, De gratia Christi Salvatoris.
